summary: Describes using MPLS multi-segment pseudowires where a passive optical network meets an MPLS network. This suits mobile backhaul, where many end nodes sit close to aggregation devices. It looks at how the segments can be handled without making those many nodes too complicated. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Many small cell towers need to connect through shared fibre to the big network. This explains how to stitch links together so a huge number of towers can join without costly equipment.

questions: how do you use pon for backhaul
how are pseudowires provisioned over pon
subtitle: Using MPLS pseudowires over passive optical networks for mobile backhaul

tldr.problem: Mobile networks have many small base stations near aggregation points. Running full MPLS routing on thousands of simple edge devices is expensive, and manually configuring each one is operationally heavy.
tldr.mechanism: The solution uses a passive optical network (PON) at the access side with simple static pseudowire configuration on the edge devices, while an MPLS network aggregates those pseudowires at a central point.
tldr.outcome: Multi-segment pseudowires allow a single service to run from a base station through a PON to an aggregation point, then through an MPLS network to a remote endpoint—without requiring complex control plane protocols on the simple edge hardware.

today: RFC 6456 is Informational and describes a practical architecture for mobile backhaul that has seen deployment in real networks. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and remains a reference for operators combining PON and MPLS technologies.

sections.title: Mobile Backhaul and Passive Optical Networks
sections.content:
Mobile backhaul networks connect base stations (cell towers) to aggregation points in the network. Traditionally, point-to-point links or simple networks connected each tower. Passive Optical Networks (PONs) offer a cost-effective alternative: many towers share a single optical fiber tree, with passive splitters at junctions and no active electronics between the tower and the central office.

However, towers often still use legacy services like Time-Division Multiplexing (TDM) or ATM. These native services must be converted to pseudowires so they can cross the PON and then the MPLS backbone network. The challenge is that the optical network units (ONUs) at the towers are cheap, simple devices with limited CPU and memory, so running full MPLS routing protocols is not feasible.
sections.plainLanguage: Many cell towers share one fiber optic cable to reach the central office. Each tower is a cheap device that only knows how to talk to the central office, not to other towers. The RFC explains how to connect native signals (like old phone circuits) across this setup and on to the wider network.

sections.title: PON Technology and G-PON / XG-PON
sections.content:
A PON consists of an Optical Line Termination (OLT) at the central office, an Optical Distribution Network (ODN) of fiber and passive splitters, and many Optical Network Units (ONUs) at customer premises. G-PON (Gigabit-capable PON) supports transmission above 1 Gbit/s, while XG-PON supports 10 Gbit/s. Both use encapsulation schemes (GEM and XGEM respectively) that support fragmentation of large frames into variable-sized transmission units.

The OLT manages the entire ODN, including allocating GEM or XGEM ports (logical connections between OLT and each ONU) and setting their bandwidth and quality of service. All management happens via OMCI, the ONT Management and Control Interface. OMCI is already required on all G-PON and XG-PON systems, so no hardware upgrade is needed to provision pseudowires this way.
sections.plainLanguage: G-PON and XG-PON are the standards for fiber networks shared by multiple customers. The central office (OLT) controls everything through a management protocol (OMCI), assigning each tower a numbered virtual connection with a bandwidth limit.

sections.title: Multi-Segment Pseudowire Architecture
sections.content:
A multi-segment pseudowire (MS-PW) is a single logical service that spans multiple network segments, each of which can be controlled differently. In the PON scenario, the first segment runs from a base station through an ONU (which acts as a Terminating Provider Edge or T-PE) to an OLT (which acts as a Switching Provider Edge or S-PE). This segment is provisioned statically using OMCI—no control plane protocols run here.

At the OLT, the service switches to a second segment that runs through the MPLS network to a remote provider edge (another T-PE). Between segments, the OLT uses penultimate hop popping (PHP) on a single-hop MPLS LSP tunnel so that no label is actually sent on the wire—the MPLS encapsulation is transparent to the PON. This allows MS-PWs to be stitched together seamlessly without requiring the ONU to understand MPLS labels.
sections.plainLanguage: The base station's signal goes to the central office (OLT) over the PON with a simple configuration. The OLT then sends it through an MPLS tunnel to the far end. From the base station's point of view, it is a single cable to the remote location, but behind the scenes it is two different network technologies.

sections.title: Provisioning and Label Management
sections.content:
The RFC specifies how pseudowire labels are provisioned on the PON end. Since ONUs lack full MPLS control plane support, labels must be assigned manually or via the management plane (OMCI). The OLT and ONU coordinate using OMCI to establish the pseudowire on the PON segment. The OLT assigns the label that will be used on the PON side and communicates it to the ONU.

At the aggregation point (OLT), the PW segment over the PON is stitched to PW segments over the MPLS PSN. The OLT may use dynamic control plane protocols (like LDP) to manage the MPLS PSN segments, while the PON segments remain statically provisioned. This hybrid approach avoids overloading the simple ONU hardware while allowing the aggregation network to operate dynamically.
sections.plainLanguage: The central office hands each tower a 'label' (a number) so the tower knows which wire its signal is on. The central office keeps track of these numbers and hooks them up to MPLS tunnels that go to the far end.
